section.title: Do Not Be Unequally Yoked
section.sectionRationale: Into the appeal for open hearts Paul sets a sharp call to separation from the defiling entanglements of an idolatrous world. Through five rhetorical contrasts he shows there can be no true partnership between righteousness and wickedness, and he grounds the call in the staggering privilege that believers are the temple of the living God, in whom God has promised to dwell. On that basis he issues the summons to come out and be separate, and the therefore of 7:1: cleanse ourselves and perfect holiness in the fear of God.
section.thesis: Because believers are the temple of the living God in whom He dwells, they must not bind themselves in compromising partnership with unbelief; rather, holding God's own promises, they are to come out, be separate, and cleanse themselves, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the command not to be unequally yoked, unfolded in five contrasts; the identity of believers as the temple of the living God with its cluster of promises; and the summons to come out and be separate, issuing in the call to perfect holiness in the fear of God.

units.label: Five contrasts that cannot be joined
units.note: no partnership between light and darkness

verses.text: Do not be {{heterozygeo|unequally yoked}} with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?
What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever?

units.label: You are the temple of the living God
units.note: I will dwell with them and be their God

verses.text: What agreement can exist between the {{naos|temple}} of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God. As God has said: “I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people.”
“Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.”
And: “I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”

units.label: Therefore perfect holiness
units.note: cleanse ourselves in the fear of God

verses.text: Therefore, beloved, since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, perfecting {{hagiosyne|holiness}} in the fear of God.

heterozygeo.gloss: To be yoked together with something of a different kind, to be mismatched in a common harness. The image recalls the law forbidding an ox and a donkey to be yoked together to plow. Paul applies it to believers binding themselves in intimate, controlling partnership with unbelievers, where the two are pulling toward opposite masters. It warns against entanglements that compromise loyalty to Christ, not against all contact with unbelievers.

naos.gloss: The temple, and specifically the inner sanctuary where God's presence dwelt, the holy place rather than the temple courts. Paul says the community of believers is the naos of the living God, the very dwelling place of His presence. This is why compromise with idols is unthinkable: the God who once filled the tabernacle and temple now dwells among and within His people. The dignity of the temple grounds the call to holiness.

hagiosyne.gloss: Holiness, the state of being set apart wholly for God. Perfecting hagiosyne is not earning acceptance but bringing to completion the consecration that belongs to those God has claimed as His temple and His sons and daughters. It is pursued in the fear of God, a reverent awe of the holy One who dwells with His people. Holiness here is both gift and calling, rooted in the promises just cited.

basic.context: Right after asking the Corinthians to open their hearts, Paul warns them not to bind themselves in compromising partnership with unbelievers. He drives it home with five sharp contrasts: righteousness and wickedness, light and darkness, Christ and Belial, believer and unbeliever, the temple of God and idols. Then he lifts their eyes to who they are: the temple of the living God, in whom God promised to dwell. On that basis he calls them to come out, be separate, and cleanse themselves, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not a call to leave the world or to shun all unbelievers, which Paul forbids elsewhere. It is a call to refuse any binding alliance where loyalty to Christ would be compromised and idolatry shared. The weight of the argument falls on identity: because you are God's temple, you cannot house idols. The chain of Old Testament promises fuels a therefore, not a fear; holiness flows from being loved and indwelt by God.
basic.originalLanguages: The command uses heterozygeo, to be yoked with a different kind, recalling the law against plowing with mismatched animals. The reason is that believers are the naos, the inner sanctuary, the dwelling place of God's presence. And the goal is hagiosyne, holiness, brought to completion in reverent fear of the God who dwells with His people.
basic.typology: The temple where God dwelt among Israel is fulfilled in the church, the living temple indwelt by His Spirit, and ultimately in Christ, the true temple. The command come out and be separate echoes the exodus from Egypt and the call out of Babylon; God's people are always a redeemed people called out to belong to Him alone.
basic.christ: Christ is set in absolute opposition to Belial: there is no harmony between them, and to belong to Christ is to be done with the works of darkness. Christ is the true temple and the one in whom God dwells with His people, and by His Spirit believers become that temple. The promises I will be their God and you will be My sons and daughters are secured in Him.
basic.god: God is the living God who dwells among His people, not a dead idol. He is the covenant Lord who promises I will be their God and they will be My people, and the Father who receives sons and daughters. He is the Lord Almighty whose holiness both welcomes and demands: He receives the separate and calls the received to perfect holiness in His fear.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 26 and Ezekiel 37 promise God dwelling among His people. Isaiah 52 is the call to come out and touch no unclean thing. First Corinthians 6 also calls the believer's body the temple of the Holy Spirit.
basic.oneStory: From Eden to the tabernacle to the temple, God has sought to dwell among His people, and sin has always threatened that dwelling. In Christ, God makes His people the temple where He lives by His Spirit, and He calls them out from idolatry to belong wholly to Him, until holiness is made complete in His presence.

context.literary:
The paragraph is a compact piece of persuasion with four parts. It begins with a command in the negative, 6:14a. It follows with five questions in a row, each answered by the silence that implies no, 6:14b to 16a. It then supplies the reason in a single claim, we are the temple of the living God, backed by a chain of quotations in 6:16b to 18. And it ends with the conclusion in 7:1, introduced by therefore, which turns the chain of promises into a call to action. The pattern is argument, then Scripture, then application.

The five questions use five different nouns for partnership: partnership, fellowship, harmony, what portion or share a believer has with an unbeliever, and agreement. They are not simply a list of synonyms; each takes the same idea from a new angle, as if Paul were looking at one stone from five sides. They also run in two pairs of abstractions, righteousness against wickedness, light against darkness, and then move to persons, Christ against Belial, believer against unbeliever, and finally to places, the temple of God against idols. So the argument moves from principles to people to the sanctuary, and the last contrast leads straight to the doctrine of the temple.

The quotations are a chain, a form sometimes called a catena. They are not separate proof texts but a blended speech in the voice of God, held together by the repeated formula says the Lord. Because 6:14 to 7:1 sits between 6:13 and 7:2, which flow on from each other, readers have long asked how it fits; the debate below takes that up. In its present place it reads as the other face of the open heart: Paul asks for room in their hearts, and then names what has to be cleared out of the temple.
context.historical:
Corinth was a trading port with many temples and a lively cult life. Meals in the temple precincts were common social occasions, and a banquet might be given to honour a god and also to mark a birth, a wedding or a business arrangement. In his earlier letter Paul had already dealt with this in detail. In 1 Corinthians 8:10 he mentions a believer reclining at table in an idol's temple, and in 10:20 to 21 he says that the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons and that one cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too.

The image of mismatched yoking has a long background. Deuteronomy 22:10 forbids ploughing with an ox and a donkey yoked together, because the two unequal animals would pull unevenly and suffer. Paul takes the picture of two parties bound to the same pole and pulling in different directions and applies it to people tied to each other by a binding commitment. In the cities of the empire, many forms of association, such as trade guilds, burial societies and patronage ties, involved ritual participation in the gods of the group, so an alliance of this kind could carry real religious cost.

The name Belial comes from a Hebrew word for worthlessness, used in the Old Testament of worthless or wicked people, for example in 1 Samuel 2:12, and in later Jewish writings it became a name for the chief of evil. Paul uses the Greek form of the name to personify the opposition to Christ, so that the choice before the Corinthians is not simply between two customs but between two lords.
context.canonical:
This short paragraph is a woven cloth of at least five Old Testament texts. The promise that God will dwell with them and walk among them takes up Leviticus 26:11 to 12 and Ezekiel 37:27, where the dwelling place is set among the people and the formula, I will be their God and they will be My people, is the language of the covenant from Exodus 29:45 onward. The call to come out and touch no unclean thing is Isaiah 52:11, spoken to those leaving Babylon who carry the vessels of the LORD. The words, I will receive you, echo the language of the return in Ezekiel 20:34 and 20:41 to 'accept' and gather the people. The last promise, I will be a Father to you, is built on 2 Samuel 7:14, where God says of David's son, I will be his father, and then widened to sons and daughters in a way that recalls Isaiah 43:6.

Taken together, they gather the covenant, the sanctuary, the exodus from exile and the promised king into one summons. The temple language also continues in the New Testament, where Paul tells the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 3:16 that they are God's temple, and in 6:19 that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and where Ephesians 2:21 to 22 says that in Christ the whole building grows into a holy temple. The picture ends at Revelation 21:3, where God Himself dwells with His people, and where the dwelling place is no longer a building but a presence.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Corinthians to take a decisive step away from anything that ties them into idol worship, and he wants them to take it because of who they are, not because of a threat. The weight of the passage falls on the sentence we are the temple of the living God. A temple is a place set apart for the presence of a deity, and a Corinthian reader would know the question instantly: what do you bring into a sacred place and what do you keep out? Paul does not hand them a rulebook. He lets the picture do the work, and then he backs it with promises, not with penalties.

He also intends the passage to lie close to his earlier correspondence, not to replace it. In the earlier letter he had said he did not mean they should leave the world, 1 Corinthians 5:9 to 10, and he had given careful teaching about mixed households, 1 Corinthians 7:12 to 14. So the command here is narrower than a general withdrawal. It addresses binding partnerships in which loyalty to Christ would be compromised and idolatry shared.

Last, the passage is not aimed at sealing the church off from people. It is aimed at the church's integrity. Paul's goal in the section is the one stated in 7:1: holiness brought to completion in the fear of God. He wants them to be distinct because that is the only way the world can see what God is like, and because his own open heart cannot be fully received by hearts still holding another lord.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The command in 6:14 is prescriptive and belongs to every generation. The quotations are descriptive of what God has promised and done, and they function as the reasons for the command, not as extra commands. The final therefore, 7:1, brings description and prescription together: because these promises are ours, we cleanse ourselves.

What is bound to the first century is the particular form of the temptation. Temple banquets and cult guilds are not on most readers' calendars, and applying the verse to every contact with unbelievers would contradict Paul's own teaching that believers live among them, 1 Corinthians 5:10. The enduring principle is to discern which alliances, whether in worship, in marriage, in business or in any binding commitment, would force a believer to share another loyalty.

The most common application is to marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, and many have read the passage that way. That is a fair extension if it is a deliberate choice to enter a binding yoke, but the text itself does not mention marriage and 1 Corinthians 7:12 to 16 tells a believer already married to an unbeliever to stay, so the passage must not be used to break existing marriages. The wise approach is to hear the principle and ask in each case what the yoke is binding and what it would cost.

debates.question: Is 6:14 to 7:1 an original part of the letter or an inserted digression?

views.label: An original Pauline digression
views.case: The passage fits Paul's argument as the demand behind the appeal to open their hearts, and the manuscripts uniformly include it here; Paul often breaks off and returns, as he does at 7:2.

views.label: A later insertion or reused fragment
views.case: Some scholars note the abrupt break between 6:13 and 7:2, distinctive vocabulary, and the dense catena of quotations, suggesting a separate piece placed here in editing.

debates.bearing: Either way the passage is canonical Scripture and functions as the sharp edge of the surrounding appeal; the call to separation and holiness stands with full authority in its present place.

debates.question: What is the scope of do not be unequally yoked?

views.label: All binding, compromising partnerships with unbelief
views.case: The five contrasts are broad, so the primary sense is any intimate alliance, business, religious, or social, in which loyalty to Christ is compromised and idolatry shared.

views.label: Chiefly marriage to an unbeliever
views.case: A long tradition applies the yoke especially to marriage, since it is the most binding of partnerships, and reads it as counsel against believers marrying unbelievers.

debates.bearing: The broad reading is primary and marriage is a clear application within it; the point is not withdrawal from all contact with unbelievers, which Paul forbids, but refusing entanglements that divide the heart from Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
Five terms in this paragraph repay close attention beyond the three the study names.

The first is the family of five nouns in 6:14 to 16. Metoche is a sharing in something held in common, as when people partner in a shared enterprise. Koinonia is fellowship or common participation, the same word used for partnership in the gospel and in the Lord's Supper. Symphonesis is harmony, from the root that gives us symphony, and it describes two voices that agree. The question what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever uses meris, a share or portion, which in other uses is a portion in an inheritance. The last is synkatathesis, agreement, a word for giving assent together with another. Paul has run through the vocabulary of partnership to show that no form of it will work.

The second is the verb in 6:16, I will dwell with them and walk among them. The Greek uses two compound verbs, enoikeo and emperipateo, in which the preposition in is attached to the root, so the sense is to make a home in them and to walk about in the midst of them. Here Paul has reworked Leviticus 26:12, where the LORD says that He will walk among the people. The text is not telling us that God visits; it says He lives in and moves about inside the community.

The third is the command in 6:17, come out and be separate, from the verbs exelthate and aphoristhete. The second verb means to mark off a boundary, to set apart, and is the ordinary verb for drawing a dividing line. In the Septuagint it also describes the LORD setting His people apart to Himself, as in Leviticus 20:26. Paul's use looks to the positive side: a people set apart for someone, not simply set apart from someone.

The fourth is the contrast between molysmos, defilement or staining, in 7:1, and katharizo, to cleanse. The word covers both body and spirit, which in the Greek is flesh and spirit, a pair that here means the whole person, outward and inward. The call is not to a ritual washing but to a thorough cleansing of conduct and inner life.

The fifth is epiteleo, to perfect or bring to completion, in 7:1. It does not mean sinless perfection; it means to carry something through to its end, like completing a building. The present participle gives the sense of continuing and carrying out the work of holiness, and the phrase in the fear of God, phobos, reaches back to 5:11, where the fear of the Lord was the motive of Paul's own ministry.

typology.type: The tabernacle and the temple, Exodus 25:8 and 1 Kings 8
typology.fulfillment: God told Moses to make a sanctuary that He might dwell among the people, and Solomon's temple became the place where His name dwelt. Both were buildings of cedar, gold and curtains, with graded holiness and a veil. Paul's claim is that the church, which was never in that building, is now where God lives by His Spirit. The correspondence is the presence of God among a covenant people. The escalation is that the presence no longer sits in a room that only priests enter but in a community of ordinary believers, and in each believer's body, 1 Corinthians 6:19. The type falls short because the old temple could be defiled from outside, and a person entering unclean could not stay; now the cleansing is by the Spirit and the blood of Christ.

typology.type: The yoke of unequal animals, Deuteronomy 22:10
typology.fulfillment: The law against ploughing with an ox and a donkey yoked together was a lesson in not binding together what is unlike. It is a small agricultural rule inside a body of law that keeps teaching Israel to keep the categories God has made. Paul uses the picture as a living image rather than a case law. The correspondence is that two partners pulling together need to share a direction. The escalation is to the moral and spiritual plane: the yoke is not a matter of animals but of ultimate loyalty. The type falls short in that the law concerns animals, not people, and it does not itself teach that believers should avoid unbelievers in ordinary life.

typology.type: The exodus and the call out of Babylon, Isaiah 52:11
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah calls those who carry the vessels of the LORD to leave Babylon, touching nothing unclean. The first exodus and the return from exile both present God's people as called out from a place where other gods ruled. Paul reads this pattern as holding for a church in a pagan city. The correspondence is a people carrying what belongs to God and needing to be clean. The escalation is that those who carry the vessels are now themselves the temple, and the leaving is not geographical. The type falls short in that Israel physically left a city, but the church stays in Corinth and is called to leave a loyalty, not a location.

God promised David that his son would be a son to Him and that He would be a father to him. In Paul's rewriting, the promise is shared out: you will be My sons and daughters. The correspondence is adoption into a royal household. The escalation is that those who belong to the Messiah share in His sonship, Galatians 4:6 and Romans 8:15, and the promise to one king becomes a promise to a people. The type falls short in that the earlier promise was to a dynasty that failed, but this one is secured by a Son who does not fail.

study.christ:
Christ appears in this paragraph in a way that is easy to miss, because his name occurs once, in the fourth question, and the rest is about God and the temple. The place to start is that question: what harmony is there between Christ and Belial? It sets the person of Christ as the pole against which every other allegiance is measured. There is no neutral middle ground, no third option. To belong to Christ is to be bound to Him, and the binding is as total as a yoke.

The second place is the temple. The Gospels present Jesus as the place where God dwells, John 1:14, and as a temple greater than the one in Jerusalem, Matthew 12:6 and John 2:19 to 21. Paul's claim that the Corinthians are the temple of the living God is a statement that they have been placed in Christ, in whom the whole building is joined together, Ephesians 2:21 to 22. The presence that rested in the holy of holies now rests in those who belong to Him. If they bring idols in, they are bringing them into the body of Christ.

The third is the way the promises are given. The statement I will be a Father to you rests on the promise to the Davidic king, and in the New Testament the title of Son belongs first to Christ. Believers share it only by being united to Him, Galatians 3:26 to 29. The sonship is therefore a fruit of the cross, not a general fact about humanity.

The fourth is that holiness is the work of Christ in us. The call to cleanse ourselves in 7:1 is a response to what He has done, since He gave Himself to redeem us and purify a people for Himself, Titus 2:14. We should not push the allegory further than the text goes. Paul does not say that Belial is a figure of any person, nor that every detail of the temple is Christ; he says plainly that Christ and Belial cannot share a house, and that the people of Christ are God's dwelling.
study.god:
The God of this paragraph is called the living God, and the title is chosen against idols, which are dead things made by hands. The phrase appears again and again in Scripture as the sharpest contrast with the gods of the nations, as in 1 Thessalonians 1:9, you turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God. That is why the argument works. A living God can live in His people; a dead idol can only be set up. The question what agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols is therefore a question about whether the living and the dead can share a room.

God is also the one who makes the promises. Every verse from 6:16 to 6:18 is introduced as His speech, and the speech is a series of I wills: I will dwell, I will be their God, I will receive you, I will be a Father to you. The grammar is that of a God who binds Himself. The call to separation sits inside His commitment and does not replace it. This matters, because it removes the fear that holiness is a condition for being loved. He gives the promises and then asks for the response.

The title Lord Almighty, in the last verse, is a title of power in the Old Testament, the LORD of hosts. The Father who is also Almighty is both tender and strong. He can receive, He can protect and He can complete the work in His sons and daughters.

Finally, the paragraph holds together God's nearness and His holiness. The God who walks among His people is the same God who says touch no unclean thing. Neither cancels the other. Holiness makes His nearness safe, because nothing unclean is let into the place where He lives, and nearness makes holiness bearable, because He is Himself the one who cleanses. Worship, then, is the response of a people who are both welcomed and set apart: awe at the presence, gratitude for the promises, and a willing clearing of the house for such a guest.

crossReferences.note: The LORD promises to make His dwelling place among His people and to walk among them, and adds that He will not despise them. This is the first source of 6:16, and its setting is the blessings of obedience. Paul takes the covenant promise and applies it to the church, which now inherits what Israel was promised.

In the vision of dry bones brought to life, God sets His sanctuary among the restored people for ever and says, My dwelling place will be with them. The text gives the second source of 6:16, set in the promise of a new covenant of peace. It shows that the dwelling is a mark of restoration and not only of law.

The call to depart, go out and touch no unclean thing is addressed to those who carry the vessels of the LORD. It is the source of 6:17. The setting is the return from exile and shows that separation is a stage in a rescue, not an end in itself.

God says of David's son, I will be his Father and he will be My son. Paul adapts the line in 6:18 by turning it into a promise for sons and daughters, which indicates how the promise to the king is shared by those who belong to Him.

The prohibition on yoking an ox and a donkey together stands behind the verb of the opening command. It shows that Paul's picture has a legal root, and that the idea of keeping unlike things from bearing the same load is old in Israel's law, not an invention of Paul.

Paul says one cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too. This is the most concrete background to the question about the temple and idols, and it explains what kind of partnership is in view: shared worship at a table of rival loyalty.

Paul says he never meant that believers must leave the world, which would mean going out of it altogether. It prevents a reading of 6:14 that demands a complete withdrawal from unbelievers, and it fixes the focus on shared allegiance rather than shared city.

Paul tells the church that they are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in them, and he warns that anyone who destroys the temple will be destroyed. It shows that the temple idea was already in his earlier teaching and that holiness protects it.

In Christ the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God in His Spirit. This is the fuller theology of the temple that 6:16 compresses, and it shows that the temple is a growing, joined community and not only a set of individuals.

The dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them as their God. This is the end of the line begun in the promise of 6:16: what is promised in part now is given in full when the new creation arrives.

study.oneStory:
Scripture begins with a sanctuary: a garden in which God walks with the man and woman in the cool of the day. It ends with a city that has no temple because God Himself and the Lamb are its temple. The story between is the story of what God does to live among a people, and of how the people keep letting something else in.

Looking back, this paragraph gathers the great moments of that story. At Sinai God gave a sanctuary so that He could dwell among them, Exodus 25:8. Solomon built a house for the name, and the prophets warned that the house could be emptied by idolatry, as Ezekiel saw the glory leave. Exile followed, and the promises of Leviticus and Ezekiel spoke of a return in which God would make His dwelling place with them again. Paul says that the promise is now coming true in a way no one had expected: not a rebuilt building but a people in whom God lives.

Looking forward, the paragraph sets up the call to holiness in the rest of the letter. It also prepares the New Testament's picture of the church as a house built of living stones, 1 Peter 2:5, in which each person is part of a single dwelling. It speaks to the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33, I will be their God and they will be My people, written on the heart.

At the end of the story the promise is complete. The loud voice from the throne announces that the dwelling place of God is with man, and the unclean and the idolater are outside, Revelation 21:8 and 27. What was once a command to come out is replaced by an open gate. The people who were called to be separate for a time are gathered in for ever, and the God who said I will receive you does so.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers?

options.text: Do not bind yourself in compromising partnership where loyalty to Christ is divided.
options.note: The yoke image warns against entanglements that share in idolatry and split the heart from Christ.

options.text: Never have any contact or friendship with unbelievers at all.
options.note: Paul elsewhere forbids total withdrawal; the issue is binding, compromising alliances.

options.text: Only that believers should worship in their own buildings.
options.note: The point is loyalty and holiness, not merely a place of worship.

options.text: That unbelievers are worthless and beneath believers.
options.note: Paul longs for unbelievers to be reconciled to God; the concern is compromise, not contempt.

quiz.q: On what basis does Paul ground his call to separation?

options.text: That believers are the temple of the living God in whom He dwells.
options.note: The identity as God's temple makes fellowship with idols unthinkable.

options.text: That unbelievers will always ruin a believer's reputation.
options.note: The ground is God's indwelling presence, not concern for reputation.

options.text: That the law of Moses forbids all mixing of peoples.
options.note: Paul cites the temple and the promises, not ethnic separation.

options.text: That separation earns a believer's salvation.
options.note: Holiness flows from being God's temple, it does not earn God's favor.

quiz.q: What promises does Paul cite to move them toward holiness?

options.text: I will dwell with them, be their God, and be a Father to them, and they will be My sons and daughters.
options.note: A chain of covenant promises of God's dwelling and adoption grounds the therefore of 7:1.

options.text: That they will become wealthy if they obey.
options.note: The promises are of God's presence and adoption, not material reward.

options.text: That they will never suffer again.
options.note: Paul has just described his own suffering; the promises are of God's dwelling, not ease.

options.text: That the law will finally be abolished.
options.note: The promises concern God's covenant presence, not the abolition of the law.

quiz.q: What is the therefore of 2 Corinthians 7:1?

options.text: Since we have these promises, cleanse ourselves and perfect holiness in the fear of God.
options.note: The promises fuel a call to complete holiness in reverent fear of God.

options.text: Since we have these promises, we may now live as we please.
options.note: The promises lead to holiness, not to license.

options.text: Since we have these promises, we should judge all unbelievers.
options.note: The call is to cleanse ourselves, not to condemn others.

options.text: Since we have these promises, holiness no longer matters.
options.note: The whole point is to perfect holiness in the fear of God.

questions: Paul warns against being unequally yoked. What binding partnerships or alliances in your life pull your loyalty away from Christ?
Believers are the temple of the living God, His dwelling place. How would truly believing that God lives in you reshape what you allow into your life?
The call to holiness rests on the promises I will be their God and you will be My sons and daughters. How does being loved and adopted by God change the way you pursue holiness?
Come out and be separate is a call to decisive action. Is there something God is asking you to walk away from in order to belong to Him alone?
Paul says to cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit. What specific defilement is God prompting you to leave behind in the fear of Him?

translationNotes.note: Unequally yoked renders heterozygeo, a mismatched yoke, echoing the law against plowing with an ox and donkey together; the sense is a binding partnership that divides loyalty, not all association with unbelievers.
Belial is a name for the evil one; the BSB footnote notes many Greek sources read Beliar, a variant spelling. Either way it names the utter opposite of Christ.
The quotations weave together Leviticus 26:12, Ezekiel 37:27, Isaiah 52:11, and 2 Samuel 7:14, set as poetry in the source and rendered here as prose within the verses, keeping the quotation marks.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 2 Corinthians 6:14-18 and 7:1. The Old Testament quotations in 6:16-18 are set as poetry in the source and rendered here as prose inside the verses, keeping the quotation marks. Sermon set to none; not verified this session.
